summary:
SMBA (Biomedical Monitoring System for Astronauts) is a web application that monitors the daily physical and psychological health of a crew during a 180-day mission. Astronauts log six blocks of daily data, including sleep, stress, mood, discomfort, blood pressure and symptoms. Ground administrators review the records, receive alerts for critical conditions, and use real data to adjust a simulation model. Each day receives a traffic-light status set by its least favorable indicator, so a single critical value is never hidden. The system keeps recorded, simulated and proposed-rule data clearly separate, and blood pressure is estimated from impedance cardiography using machine learning.

The project addresses the challenge of detecting health risks early when crews are far from Earth and medical help is delayed. It matters because early detection of problems such as blood pressure changes, fluid shifts, isolation stress and radiation exposure can help prevent serious health issues before they happen. The alert thresholds are proposals that still require medical validation.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
It is a web application that monitors a crew’s health every day during a 180-day mission, organized in 5-day cycles. Each day, the astronaut logs six blocks of data: sleep, stress, mood, discomfort, exercise and blood pressure, and general symptoms. Each day gets a traffic-light status (green, yellow or red) based on its least favorable indicator. The ground administrator reviews the records, receives alerts for red days, and can use real data to adjust the simulation.

What benefits does it offer?
It helps detect health changes early, when the crew is far from Earth and help takes time to arrive. It keeps recorded data, simulated data and proposed rules clearly separate, so they are not confused. It works offline, stores records on the device and syncs them later. It also asks for very few permissions: no camera, microphone, location or Bluetooth.

What is the expected impact?
It aims to help prevent health problems in astronauts, such as blood pressure changes, fluid shifts, isolation stress or radiation exposure, before they get worse. The thresholds still need medical validation, so the real impact depends on that validation.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Platform: the prototype is published with Enter (enter.converge.ai), which provides the shared database and account identity.
  • Prediction models: linear regression for systolic pressure and support vector machines (SVR) for diastolic pressure, trained on impedance cardiography (ICG) variables.
  • Presentation and report: pptxgenjs for the slides and docx for the report.
  • Hardware: no special equipment is needed, just a browser on a computer or phone.

Pending confirmation from the team: the exact frontend and backend programming languages, and the version of the machine learning models.

In what sense is your project creative?

  • It combines daily logging, a traffic-light status and alerts in a single view, so the astronaut and the administrator understand the day’s status at a glance.
  • It uses gamification (points, levels such as Cadet or Health Commander, and achievements) to encourage consistent daily logging.
  • It simulates complete missions in a reproducible way, including high blood pressure episodes and solar storms, so the system can be tested before real data is available.

What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA standards: the stress and mood baseline follows the Isolation Standard Measures (ISM).
  • Prior research: the pressure model is compared with the IAC-25 study and was deliberately tuned to fall below its accuracy, without being presented as clinical accuracy.
  • Privacy and minimum permissions.
  • Real-world use: offline operation, and it is designed for phones, although mobile screen testing is still pending.
  • Honesty about limitations: simulated data and proposed rules are clearly distinguished from real records.
